title: Country musicians who came to New Orleans: Humphrey, Robichaud, Celestin
summary: He recalls his father's accounts of old man Humphrey teaching in the country and of musicians such as John Robichaud and Celestin coming to the city from rural places to find work.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, I'm mad because from what my, my dad remembers, quite a fellow's, a musician that came here, from different parts of, out of New Orleans. See, they would, they would hear about New Orleans, and they'd probably, in fact, I remember dad used to tell me about, uh, old man, Ompren, the fathers are the one now. Mm-hmm. Said he used to go out in those countries and teach.

And he used to, uh, make his money by paying him somebody for teaching and selling them instruments and writing their, their music. You know, instructing their music for them and teach the brass band and instruct them private and everything. Said he made a lot of his money that way. And that's how I imagine a lot of the fellas after they learned and everything and they heard somebody talk about New Orleans after they learned how to play, they'd want to come to New Orleans and, and, and get work, see? And find a way, cause I remember like, uh, uh, uh, Bebe Rizzling. My dad, I remember when he first come here. And, uh, cause he was from on, uh, like on the outskirt. And then another man, John Robich, with a left hand violin player, he used to play in the lyrics theater. My dad used to keep him by then. He said he came to New Orleans playing an accordion. I remember the little, they call him a, a wind jammer. Wind jammer. I think it's a wind jammer or something. Yeah. He said he brought him up to see Dave Perkin. He said Dave Perkin laughed at him. He said, man, you can't make no money with that. He got, you got to play some kind of instrument. So I don't know how he, well, he learned violin when he came here, but I knew he was, he, he was a violin player. And my daddy played with him quite a bit. And then there was, uh, another fellow. He was, uh, responsible of, of having, uh, what they call, uh, one of the, uh, famous Negro, uh, uh, uh, uh, uh, club, uh, uh, uh, let's see what you call that. Society. In other words, he came here as a, as a waiter. And he got with the rich, good, rich people. And through being a waiter, through John Robichaud, he got the job for the musician. So that's how John got his start. And today is, is, uh, it's, it's a club now, young man twenties, I believe. And this man used to, used to have, uh, little things on weekends for the people that wanted to learn how to dance. All the colored people wanted to learn how to dance. And, uh, they would have their things in any form of clubs. And that's responsible of, of the, of the young, I think it's the young man twenties. One of those big colored things we have right now. That's how they started. And, uh, what we're going back to, uh, to, uh, John, uh, yeah, John Robichaud. Yeah. How he came here. And, uh, there's another fellow. He didn't even know how, when, when Celestan came here from out of the country. Where did he come from? Well, I can't think exactly right now, what time, but I know he remember when he, when he first came here.
Somebody mentioned that Froggy Moore once, that he was up there. What was that little suburb, little town, village? Froggy Moore.
I remember there was a place called, like I said, from Donnellsville, where they called Froggy Moore from Donnellsville.
